data.title: The Big Picture: When The Math Finally Breaks
data.description:
If you’ve been listening to our broadcast over the years, you know I often remind our listeners of an old rule of thumb: Wall Street is paid to sell you the next hot story, but math is the only thing that never lies.

Right now, the financial press is obsessed with the AI bust and the Fed’s next move. Will they raise rates a quarter or half a point in December? Will that be followed by further hikes in January and March? Currently, the futures market is forecasting a 97% quarter-point increase in December, a 70% quarter-point hike in January, and a 46% quarter-point rise in March. But the market is probably going to force a pivot.

If you step back from the current headlines and look at the big picture, the more important story isn’t really about the Fed or even AI. It’s that the U.S. government is heading straight into a wall of debt refinancing in 2027—and the numbers simply no longer add up.

The 2027 Debt “Maturity Wall”

Imagine a family that went on a massive spending spree back in 2020. Fortunately for them, the bank offered a special introductory promotion: zero-percent interest for five years.

For five years, that family felt rich. They bought whatever they wanted, and their monthly credit card statement looked tiny because their interest rate was practically zero.

Then the promotion ends. The teaser rate expires, and the bank informs them that their borrowing rate is now adjusting to 22%.

Suddenly, even if they don’t buy another single thing, their monthly interest payment alone eats up half their paycheck.

Sound familiar? What happened to homeowners in the 2000s is precisely what is now happening to the U.S. government.

During the 2020–2021 pandemic crisis, the Treasury borrowed trillions of dollars at rock-bottom rates between 0.5% and 1.8%.

Now those 5-year and 7-year IOUs are coming due.

Through the rest of this year, over $1.1 trillion in older, low-rate debt has to be paid off and replaced with brand-new debt.

In 2027, the dam really breaks: approximately $3.4 trillion in medium- and long-term notes come due. When you include short-term Treasury bills, the government will have to roll over close to $9 trillion in a single year.

Here’s the catch: the Treasury can’t borrow at 1% anymore. Today, it must pay close to 5% or more.

For twenty-five years, whenever Uncle Sam rolled over old debt, it did so at lower rates. Monthly payments went down. Today, that dynamic has flipped. Refinancing that mountain of debt at today’s rates adds tens of billions of dollars every single year to the deficit purely through higher interest costs.

The Snowball Effect: Looking at the Real Numbers

In fiscal year 2026, total government spending topped $7.4 trillion. But look at where that money went: net interest on the national debt jumped over 11% to roughly $1.14 trillion. Net interest is now bigger than our entire national defense budget.

Entitlements are on autopilot: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid ate up another huge chunk of the budget.

According to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO), our total national debt is blowing past $40 trillion this year. By 2030, debt held by the public will cross 108% of GDP.

To put that into historical perspective: the highest debt level America ever reached was 106% of GDP in 1946, right after mobilizing the entire nation to fight and win World War II. We are on track to permanently shatter that wartime record in peacetime—with no world war, no national draft, and no emergency mobilization.

By 2036, the CBO projects interest payments alone will cross $2.1 trillion a year. At that point, Social Security, healthcare programs, and interest on the debt will consume virtually every single penny of federal taxes collected. Every other department—from the military to the FBI to national parks—will have to be put on the national credit card.

Why Washington Won’t Fix It

You might ask: won’t politicians in Washington just cut spending or raise taxes to fix this?

I’ve watched Washington for over forty years in my career. Neither party has the stomach for real fiscal discipline.

When you look at the major spending proposals on Capitol Hill—whether it’s expanded family tax credits, universal childcare subsidies, healthcare expansions, or housing grants—we are looking at another $3.6 to $4.4 trillion in gross spending programs over the next decade.

Even if you pass every proposed tax increase on corporations and high earners, it barely makes a dent against the compounding wave of interest and baby-boomer retirements. The structural annual deficit will still run at nearly 6% of GDP as far as the eye can see.

The Economy Today: A Tale of Two Consumers

Now let’s look at the economy. Are we about to fall into a deep recession tomorrow?

The economic indicators we watch—like the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index (LEI)—are actually telling us that growth is holding up around 2%. The job market isn’t falling off a cliff.

Instead, we have a two-track, K-shaped economy.

The Strained Main Street Consumer: If you make an average paycheck, life feels expensive. Prices are up anywhere from 30% to 50% (or higher) since 2020. Credit card debt is at record highs, car loan delinquencies are climbing, and mortgage rates above 7% have frozen the housing market.

The Booming Industrial and AI Pipeline: On the other side of the tracks, money is pouring into artificial intelligence data centers, rebuilding our aging electrical power grid, domestic energy production, and military manufacturing.

This capital-spending boom is keeping the economy afloat. But it has a weak spot: it requires enormous amounts of cheap electricity, expensive equipment, and heavy borrowing. If interest rates stay high, those big corporate projects will eventually hit a wall, too.

The Big Question: When Does the Fed Blink?

Wall Street consensus says the Fed will start cutting rates by mid-2027 because inflation will magically drift down to its 2% target.

I don't buy that inflation story, and neither do many of the sharp macro thinkers we follow.

They point out that the Fed is trapped in a condition economists call Fiscal Dominance. In plain English: the government’s debt has grown so massive that the central bank can no longer control the steering wheel.

Think about the trap Fed Chairman Warsh is in.

If he keeps rates high to fight inflation, he bankrupts the Treasury by forcing them to refinance trillions of dollars at 5%, while crushing regional banks and corporate borrowers.

If he slashes rates, he pours gasoline on inflation, crude oil spikes higher, and consumer prices take off again.

Furthermore, Luke Gromen points out an incredible paradox: when debt is this high, high interest rates fuel inflation. Why? Because the federal government is paying out over $1.1 trillion in cash interest directly into the financial system, putting fresh purchasing power right back into circulation!

So, what happens next? Grant Williams describes it as a forced capitulation. The Fed won’t cut rates because they “won” the inflation fight. No, they will cut rates because the Treasury market will force them to.

We’ve seen this movie before. In the late 1940s, after World War II, the U.S. government had a 106% debt-to-GDP problem. Did they raise interest rates to 10% to fight inflation? Absolutely not.

The Fed stepped in and capped interest rates at 2.5%, while inflation ran at 6%, 8%, or even 10%.

That is called Financial Repression. The government intentionally holds interest rates below the rate of inflation, slowly eroding the purchasing power of cash and bonds to shrink the debt in real terms. It’s a hidden tax on every saver in America.

Your Survival Guide: How to Invest for What Lies Ahead

So, how do you protect yourself when the game is rigged to erode paper money?

For decades, the standard advice was the “60/40 portfolio”—put 60% of your money in stocks and 40% in government bonds, then sit back and retire. In an era of fiscal dominance, that strategy is broken. Long-term government bonds yielding less than the real cost of living are guaranteed to lose purchasing power.

The Financial Playbook My Firm Is Following for Clients

  1. Own Businesses with Real Cash Flow, Not Promises
    In a high-rate world, companies that don’t make money today are toxic. Move money away from debt-heavy, speculative tech stocks trading at nosebleed valuations. Focus on Defensive Value: Healthcare, Consumer Staples, Utilities. These are companies that sell everyday necessities, generate hard cash today, and pay reliable dividends.

  2. Overweight Energy and Master Resources
    Energy is the lifeblood of everything we do. Between geopolitical strife in the Middle East and the massive electric power demanded by new AI data centers, global energy supplies are tight. Owning oil, gas, and power infrastructure gives your portfolio an ironclad inflation hedge.

  3. Demand Clean Balance Sheets
    Avoid companies drowning in junk debt. When that 2027 refinancing wall hits corporate America, weaker businesses will see their profit margins crushed by higher interest costs. Stick with companies with little to no debt and ample cash reserves.

  4. Don’t Panic into 100% Cash
    A lot of frightened investors throw their hands in the air and move everything into cash. That’s a mistake. While cash pays a decent nominal return today, financial repression guarantees that inflation will outrun cash over time. Plus, with corporate share buybacks running hot and short-sellers heavily short, markets can stage violent rallies when you least expect it.

  5. Hold Real, Tangible Assets: Gold
    If history teaches us one undeniable lesson, it is this: whenever governments find themselves with too much debt, they always choose to debase the currency. They have done it from ancient Rome to 18th-century France to post-WWII America.

Physical gold is nobody’s liability. It cannot be printed by a central bank, and it cannot be defaulted on by a politician. In an age of financial repression, gold remains the ultimate monetary anchor.

The Bottom Line

You don’t need to fear the future, but you do need to understand the rules of the game we are playing.

The 2026–2027 debt wall is a mathematical certainty. Washington cannot borrow trillions of dollars forever without consequences, and the Federal Reserve will eventually be forced to choose between defending its currency or bailing out the Treasury.

Keep your head clear, tune out the daily market cheerleaders, avoid debt-choked companies, and anchor your wealth in tangible, cash-flowing assets.

Until next time, stay disciplined, stay safe, and always keep your eye on the Big Picture.

data.title: The Index Looks Fine. The Heat Map Does Not.
data.description:
WallStreetBets does not usually hand you a clean research note. Last night it handed everyone a giant red rectangle.

A Discussion post titled Last 4-month heat map blew up with roughly 4,000 upvotes and hundreds of comments. The picture is the familiar market map: boxes sized by company size, colored by how far prices have moved, and almost every box is blood red. Nvidia (NVDA) sits near 40% below its recent high, while memory names, chip-equipment stocks, and storage names look even worse. Google (GOOGL), Oracle (ORCL), and Caterpillar (CAT) got painted with the same brush.

The original poster put the quiet part in plain English. This has been a crash under the hood, even if the S&P 500 has not tagged a clean 10% drop yet. That line is the whole argument, and my take lines up with it. The headline index can still look like a messy correction while the engine room of this bull market is already in full drawdown. If your portfolio lives in the red boxes, the map is telling you the truth faster than the S&P number on cable.

What the map is actually showing

People argue about start dates on these charts, and they should. A fixed calendar return from July is not the same thing as a fall from each stock's own high over the last few months. When you line the big tiles up against real prices, the honest read is closer to peak-to-now pain inside a roughly four-month window of highs.

Nvidia topped near $239 in early October and recently traded near $146, about a 40% hole from that high. The semiconductor ETF that tracks the group is still roughly a third below its June peak. Intel (INTC) and ARM are about 60% off their early-summer highs, and Sandisk is on the order of two-thirds lower from its June spike. Micron (MU) and the big equipment names that feed the fabs fill in more of the damage.

Now put the polite index next to that mess. The S&P 500, through SPY, is only about 8% under its early-October high near $779. The Nasdaq-100 path is uglier, down about 15% from the same peak week, and the Dow has slipped back under 50,000. None of those index moves match the temperature of a map where the largest technology tiles look like a stop sign. Indexes are averages with weights, so a handful of survivors can keep the headline from looking like a crash while the prior leadership gets cut in half. That gap is the story.

The survivors are doing real work

Look past the loudest red boxes and you can see why the S&P still has people arguing. Apple (AAPL) has barely given back its recent high and is still solidly up on the year. Microsoft (MSFT) has been one of the adult names in the room on a multi-month calendar view even after a pullback from its own peak, and Amazon (AMZN) has been choppy rather than ruined. Those weights matter, because when the biggest household names hold up better than the speculative AI stack, the index can grind lower without ever looking like 2022 on a chart you glance at once a day.

Breadth can rot while the brand-name average keeps its dignity, which is how investors get talked into thinking they own "the market" when they really own last year's winners at this year's prices. Wall Street will call it healthy rotation. Sometimes rotation is real, and sometimes it is a polite word for the old leadership breaking while a few mega-caps still pay the rent for the index.

Why the under-the-hood crash matters

I am not calling for a cartoon collapse from here, and I am not telling you to light your account on fire. I am saying the heat map is a better dashboard than a single percentage on the S&P.

If the bull market of the last few years was sold as an artificial-intelligence buildout story, then Nvidia, memory, equipment, and the software hanging off that spend are not side shows. They are the plot. A world where those names are down 30% to 60% from their highs while commentators shrug at an 8% index drawdown is a world where risk already showed up, and it showed up first in the places that ran the hardest.

The useful part of the Reddit thread is the admission that index calm and portfolio pain can live in the same month. For anyone holding stocks through this, the practical questions are boring on purpose. How much of what you own is the red cluster on that map? How much leverage, direct or through products that sell when volatility rises, sits on top of those names? Do you still have cash if the under-the-hood crash runs longer than the cable segment about it? Forced sellers do not wait for a perfect bear-market label. They sell when the collateral math says sell.

Watch the falsifiers, not the hot takes. If credit stays orderly while chips thrash, you are often watching a leadership break and a positioning unwind. If credit cracks and the index ballast names finally join the red sea, the under-the-hood story becomes everybody's problem. If Apple-and-Microsoft-class ballast keeps holding the average together while the AI stack stabilizes on real earnings rather than hope, the map can heal from the inside without a full capitulation speech.

Bottom Line

The WallStreetBets heat map is loud because it is honest. The S&P can sit about 8% under its peak and still hide a real crash in the AI and semiconductor engine that powered the rally. Trust the red boxes you actually own more than the polite index percentage on TV, and know your leverage before the next leg decides it for you.

data.title: Pound Under Pressure As GBP/USD Tests Yearly Lows
data.description:
GBP/USD fell to 1.3085 on Friday, remaining at its lowest level in almost a year. The main pressure on the pound comes from sharply rising expectations of further Fed tightening, which is supporting the US dollar.

Minutes from the October Fed meeting showed that the Fed is increasingly concerned about persistent inflation and acknowledges the need for additional rate hikes. Policymaker Christopher Waller called for more decisive action if price pressures continue to rise. Markets now estimate the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December at 97.3%, with the chance of a 50-basis-point move at 2.7%.

In the UK, the situation is less straightforward. The Bank of England expects inflation to accelerate further by mid-2027 due to cumulative cost pressures, but some components of the October CPI proved fairly stable. Against this backdrop, markets have scaled back expectations of a BoE rate hike in December, further limiting support for the pound.

Yields on UK government bonds also fell following the inflation report, with the yield on 10-year gilts dropping to 5.29%. Although headline CPI reached 3.6% year-on-year, markets have become more cautious about further Bank of England tightening, adding to pressure on GBP/USD.

October UK retail sales will be the next key release, with zero month-on-month growth and 1.7% year-on-year growth expected. Stronger-than-expected data could temporarily support the pound, but the fundamental balance remains in the dollar’s favour due to much stronger expectations of Fed tightening.

Technical Analysis

The H4 GBP/USD chart remains in a downtrend. After a reversal in early November, the pair has formed a succession of lower highs and lows while remaining within the descending channel. The MACD signal line is below zero and pointing downwards, indicating continued downward momentum. The nearest target on H4 is 1.3024.

On the H1 GBP/USD chart, the pair rebounded from 1.3078 to approach 1.3125, where it had previously consolidated. For Friday, 20 November 2026, the baseline scenario assumes a test of 1.3125 from below. If resistance holds, a return to 1.3078 is likely. A break below this low would open the way towards 1.3024. Both Stochastic oscillator lines are above 80. A move out of the overbought zone would strengthen the signal for a resumption of the decline, with the 20 mark becoming the next reference point for the oscillator.

After reaching 1.3024, a rebound towards 1.3080 is possible. If the recovery is limited to this area, the next local downside target is 1.2980. This level corresponds to the continuation of the wave on H4 and may be reached beyond Friday’s session. The longer-range target of the downward wave, based on the chart markings, lies at 1.2584 and remains relevant while the trend holds. A close above 1.3125 on the hourly chart would postpone the intraday decline scenario and increase the likelihood of a deeper correction. In that case, the nearest recovery target would be the high of the previous upward move on the hourly chart, formed on 19 November.

Conclusion

GBP/USD has fallen to its lowest level in almost a year, weighed down by sharply rising expectations of further Fed tightening, with December rate hike probabilities now at 97.3% for a 25-basis-point move. While the Bank of England also expects inflation to accelerate, stable components in the October CPI and falling gilt yields have led markets to scale back BoE rate hike expectations, further weighing on the pound. The fundamental balance remains firmly in the dollar’s favour. Technically, the downtrend is intact, with resistance at 1.3125 and support at 1.3078 and 1.3024. A break below 1.3078 would open the way towards 1.3024 and potentially 1.2980, with the longer-range target at 1.2584. A close above 1.3125 would postpone the decline scenario and point to a deeper correction. October UK retail sales will be the next catalyst for the pair.

data.title: Preliminary Regional Fed Manufacturing Reports Suggest Inflation Is Spreading Downstream
data.description:
In discussing the ISM manufacturing index several weeks ago, I concluded that it “reminded me of the regional Fed reports for the last month, which suggested that while the expansion is intact, the second derivative may be declerating, i.e., the rate of growth has been peaking; and further that its inflationary component is accelerating, which is not good for downstream consumer prices.”

Here’s what the new orders component of that index looked like:

Well, now we have three regional Fed bank reports for November: New York, Philadelphia, and Kansas City, which give us our first look at how manufacturing is doing this month. The first two do get picked up by FRED, so let’s see what their averages can tell us.

First of all, the headline numbers (bue) declined -6.2 to 7.0, which suggests at least that the growth rate is stabilizing and possibly decelerating somewhat.  But, unlike the ISM report at the beginning of this month, the average of the new orders component (red) was the lowest since last year, as it decelerated sharply, by -12.4, to 1.3:

Meanwhile, the respective numbers from the Kansas City Fed constrasted significantly, as the headline regional index rose 7 to 18, and the new orders component rose 13 to 16.

Put all three together and the picture is of a stabilizing topline, and at very least the proverbial bloom might be coming off the rose somewhat as to new orders.

There might be an even more significant amplification present is in the prices component, and specifically prices received from downstream customers (red in the graph below). Prices paid declined -1.3 to 52.0, suggesting the torrid spread of price increases in that component has persisted. But even more signficantly, prices received rose 1.2 to 37.1. The last two months have been the highest readings in that entire series since the start of the Millennium outside of the post-pandemic period:

The regional Kansas City index suggested the same, with prices paid declining -17 to 53, and prices received rising 4 to 30.

In short, producers appear more determined, and able, to pass on higher prices to downstream customers, suggesting that consumer inflation, at least in the goods sector, is not going to slow in the next several months, and may even increase further. And keep in mind that real aggregate nonsupervisory payrolls may go negative YoY as early as next month if there is such a pass-through of inflation and a tepid employment report. In that regard, the best news in the surveys was that employment average rose 5.4 to 1.8:

All well and good for the present, but if corporate profits come under pressure, and real wages come under pressure as well, needless to say that would not be good.

data.title: Palo Alto Networks Stock Soars On Strong FCF Guidance - Any More Upside Left In PANW?
data.description:
Palo Alto Networks (PANW), a cybersecurity software subscription company, reported strong free cash flow (FCF) margins and guided to 38% this fiscal year. PANW stock rose 8% on this guidance on Thursday after rising ahead of the results. Could it be worth more?

PANW is at $364.77, up more than 7.0% midday on Thursday, Nov. 19, after rising 9.9% on Wednesday from a recent low of $309.29 on Nov. 17 ahead of the Nov. 18 fiscal Q1 2027 earnings release (ending Oct. 31) after the market closed.

PANW stock - last 3 months - Barchart - Nov. 19, 2026

Moreover, analysts seem to be very positive on the stock. For example, Yahoo! Finance reports that the average price target (PT) of 54 analysts is $405.78, and Barchart's mean survey PT is $398.62. These PTs are only about 8% higher than Thursday's price (11/19).

So, is there much upside left in PANW?

FCF performance and high FCF Margin Guidance

Palo Alto Networks' fiscal Q1 revenue was up 39.25% YoY, and over the past year it rose 30.29%, according to Stock Analysis data.

Moreover, its adjusted free cash flow (FCF rose 13.1% to $1.937 billion YoY. However, its adj. FCF margin fell from 69.2% in Q1 last year to 59.6% in fiscal Q1 2027.

Nevertheless, on a trailing 12-month (TTM) basis (which is important since many of its clients renew subscriptions annually), the adj. FCF rose almost $1 billion from last year.

This can be seen on page 31 of its presentation deck. It shows that TTM adj. FCF rose from $3.75 billion last year to $4.638 billion in Q1 (+23.5%). It was even 5% higher than the Q4 TTM figure.

Palo Alto Networks - Adj. FCF trailing 12 months (TTM) - Q1 deck page 31 - Nov. 18, 2026

Note, however, that the TTM adj. FCF margin dipped slightly to 37.3% from 39.3% of revenue last year and even 38.4% in fiscal Q4.

However, management provided a 38.0% adj. FCF guidance for the year ending July 31, 2027. Let's see how that might work out. 

Forecasting FCF and Price Targets

Management expects its revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion. That's even higher than prior analysts' average forecasts of $14.4 billion.

For the next year, these analysts forecast $16.47 billion in revenue. So, over the next 12 months (NTM), revenue could be about $15 billion:

  $14.55b x 0.75 + $16.47b x 0.25 = $10.91b +$4.12b = $15.02 billion NTM revenue

So, applying a 38% margin, adj. FCF could hit $5.708 billion

That's over $1 billion higher than the $4.638 billion TTM figure shown above. In other words, its forecasted NTM adj. FCF could rise over 23%.

That certainly shows why the stock is up so much. But, how much is left?

For example, Palo Alto Networks' adj. FCF yield has averaged about 2.0% over the last year (i.e., a 50x multiple). So, applying this metric to its NTM adj. FCF forecast:

  $5.708 / 0.02 = $285.4 billion fair value

That's only about 2.5% above its present market cap of $278.32 billion today. And that implies a PT of $372.30. That's lower than other analysts' targets, as I showed above.

Even with a slightly better 1.85% FCF yield (i.e., a 54x multiple), the stock is worth just $308.54 billion, or +10.9% higher. That gives it a NTM price target of $402.81.

Summary and Conclusion

Palo Alto Networks produced strong adj. FCF with lower quarterly margins, including slightly lower TTM adj. FCF as a percent of revenue (37.3%). As a result, with management's guidance of 38% margin this year and applying this to a next 12-month (NTM) revenue forecast, its adj. FCF could hit $5.7 billion.

With a generous 54x multiple, that only implies a 10.9% higher price target for Palo Alto Networks. Nevertheless, the stock could exceed this at any time. 

But value investors have to take this into account when deciding whether its recent rise leaves any upside.

data.title: Inflation Takes On A Life Of Its Own Independent Of Oil Prices
data.description:
Driving by the local gas station, motorists are taking a sigh of relief as pump prices have declined rapidly in recent weeks—-- a reflection in the hope for a US-Iranian peace agreement will put  an end  to the disruptions in the oil market. Bond investors, reacting to the prospects of future inflation, however continue to drive up yields, and central bankers talk up the need to curb inflation with higher rates for longer. The once tight correlation between oil prices, inflation and government bonds is coming apart. 

Historically, oil price shocks, such as those in the 1970s and 1980s, had an immediate effect of driving up prices across the board. At the same time, the drop in oil prices resulted in a rapid decline in the rate of inflation—-- a sharp doubled-edge sword. Today, inflation expectations  seem to be well-anchored, such that despite a drop in the oil prices, consumer inflation seems very slow to react, putting central bankers on alert towards raising rates.

Earlier in the year, the  tight correlation between oil and government borrowing costs has defined global bond markets,as the long end of the credit markets everywhere hit highs not experienced in over a decade. So, central bankers blamed the geopolitical situation for the need  to raise rates, emanating from the Iranian conflict. But that conflict is in abeyance and oil is now flowing through the Straits of Hormuz close to pre-war levels 

Starting in 2022,  the correlation between oil prices and interest rates averaged around 25%, yet interest rates climbed steadily from 1.8% to 4%, as central banks moved off the ultra-low rates that characterized the 2020s. With the advent of the Iranian conflict,  oil prices spiked from $65/bbl to $120/bb, accompanied by a surge in  the 10-year yield  from 4.2% to 5.1%. Current estimates put the oil-interest rate  correlation at 20%-25%.

But despite steep falls in global crude benchmarks in recent weeks — in part on hopes for US-Iran peace talks — yields and expectations for rate rises have remained elevated, keeping up the pressure on governments’ and households’ finances. Central banks are focusing on a raft of conditions to guide their deliberations, and the oil prices seem to play a lesser role in their minds. Inflation is no longer confined to specific commodities, but is more generally pervasive, pushing the central bankers to tighten further.
